info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 6.3: AI-Assisted Normalization and the Risk of Over-Normalization.

name.text: 01 Question: Today's Question: Capability vs. Fidelity

questiontext.text: What is the central methodological challenge when digital editors introduce generative AI into historical text normalization?

generalfeedback.text: Generative AI brings powerful contextual reasoning to text normalization, but editors must actively prevent uncritical modernization and over-normalization.

answer.text: Balancing the model's powerful contextual reasoning against the risk of uncritical modernization, silent rewrites, and loss of editorial transparency.

feedback.text: Correct. AI brings contextual disambiguation that rules lack, but risks over-normalizing historical voices unless tightly audited and constrained.

answer.text: Ensuring the AI can translate 18th-century English into modern Mandarin Chinese.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text normalization regularizes historical orthography within the same language, not translation into foreign tongues.

answer.text: Proving that generative AI models are legally incapable of processing TEI XML markup.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language models process XML markup easily; the challenge is editorial fidelity and control.

answer.text: Eliminating all human editors so that archives can transcribe documents without staff.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative AI is an editorial assistant that requires rigorous human oversight, not an unmonitored replacement.

name.text: 02 Question: From Sequence-to-Sequence Models to Modern Generative LLMs

questiontext.text: Why does an off-the-shelf generative Large Language Model (LLM) pose a distinct risk of over-normalization compared to older character-level models?

generalfeedback.text: Modern generative LLMs possess vast latent knowledge of historical spelling, but their training toward modern fluency predisposes them to over-normalize historical texts.

answer.text: LLMs are optimized on modern web text and RLHF to produce fluent, modern prose, naturally defaulting toward rewriting rather than conservative preservation.

feedback.text: Correct. Commercial LLMs have a strong generative bias toward modern fluency, which can flatten historical linguistic nuances unless explicitly restrained.

answer.text: Modern LLMs have a vocabulary limited to fewer than 500 English words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs have vocabularies spanning tens of thousands of subword tokens across multiple languages.

answer.text: LLMs cannot read text files unless they have been converted to raster images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs operate directly on text and token sequences.

answer.text: Older character-level models possessed human-level historical consciousness.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Character models lacked semantic understanding; they were simply constrained by narrow statistical transitions.

name.text: 03 Question: The Contextual Advantage: Disambiguating Homographs

questiontext.text: What unique contextual advantage does a generative LLM possess over a deterministic regex pattern like \b([Dd])roit\b?

generalfeedback.text: LLMs use contextual self-attention to successfully disambiguate syntactic homographs (like droit vs. etoit) that trip up global regex rules.

answer.text: Self-attention allows the LLM to inspect surrounding syntax and distinguish between an invariable legal noun (le droit) and an archaic verb form (il droit / droit -> doit).

feedback.text: Correct. Transformer models attend across surrounding words to determine parts of speech and grammatical function, avoiding blind global substitutions.

answer.text: The LLM can physically alter the ink chemistry on the historical parchment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs manipulate digital representations, not physical artifacts.

answer.text: The LLM guarantees 100% mathematical zero-error execution on every search.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs are probabilistic models, whereas regex is mathematically deterministic.

answer.text: A regex pattern automatically rewrites all French vocabulary into Latin.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regex replaces only what its literal pattern specifies.

name.text: 04 Question: The Critical Risk: Over-Normalization

questiontext.text: What constitutes 'over-normalization' in digital scholarly editing?

generalfeedback.text: Over-normalization occurs when an AI model exceeds spelling regularization to silently alter historical vocabulary, syntax, or authorial style.

answer.text: When an automated tool exceeds historical orthographic regularization and alters legitimate archaic vocabulary, syntax, or authorial style.

feedback.text: Correct. Normalization regularizes spelling; over-normalization silently corrupts historical syntax, vocabulary, or dialectal authenticity.

answer.text: When an editor applies TEI XML tags to more than five words per paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rich encoding is encouraged; over-normalization refers to inappropriate textual alteration.

answer.text: When a file is saved in UTF-8 encoding instead of ASCII.

feedback.text: Incorrect. UTF-8 is the required standard encoding for digital humanities editions.

answer.text: When an editor uses git commit messages that exceed fifty characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commit message formatting is a repository practice, not a textual editorial error.

name.text: 05 Question: The Hypercorrection Taxonomy in Normalization

questiontext.text: Which error category in the normalization taxonomy occurs when an AI replaces an authentic archaic word like 'hath' with 'has', or 'unto' with 'to'?

generalfeedback.text: Classify AI normalization errors using the four-part taxonomy: lexical substitution, morphological modernization, semantic hallucination, and syntactic restructuring.

answer.text: Lexical and grammatical modernization.

feedback.text: Correct. Substituting a modern grammatical auxiliary or preposition for an authentic historical form constitutes grammatical modernization, violating editorial policy.

answer.text: Hallucinated abbreviation expansion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hallucinated expansion refers to inventing words inside an abbreviation tag, not modernizing authentic words.

answer.text: Milestone tag deletion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Milestone tag deletion involves dropping structural tags like .

answer.text: Punctuation leveling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation leveling refers to replacing dashes or colons with modern commas or periods.

name.text: 06 Question: Hallucinated Abbreviation Expansions

questiontext.text: Why is an AI expansion like w^chwhich was agreed upon a severe editorial failure?

generalfeedback.text: An tag must contain only the omitted letters of the abbreviated word; verify that AI models never inject explanatory glosses or phantom clauses.

answer.text: The tag must supply only the exact omitted letters of the abbreviated word itself, not editorial explanatory commentary or extra clauses.

feedback.text: Correct. Abbreviations represent specific historical words; adding extra narrative words turns an abbreviation expansion into an uncontrolled hallucination.

answer.text: The word 'which' is illegal in TEI XML documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 'Which' is a valid word; the error is adding extra words not present in the contraction.

answer.text: TEI guidelines mandate that tags must always be written in uppercase.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI element names are case-sensitive and must be written in lowercase.

answer.text: Superscript letters cannot be enclosed in XML tags under any circumstances.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Superscripts are commonly encoded using or inside .

name.text: 07 Question: Negative Prompting: The Essential Defense

questiontext.text: What role does negative prompting play when instructing an LLM to normalize historical texts?

generalfeedback.text: Negative prompting is the digital editor's primary defense: explicitly forbid lexical substitution, grammatical modernization, and stylistic smoothing.

answer.text: It explicitly establishes forbidden transformations, preventing the model from modernizing vocabulary, rewriting syntax, or flattening idiosyncratic style.

feedback.text: Correct. Generative models naturally tend toward modern fluency; negative constraints are required to actively suppress helpful rewriting behaviors.

answer.text: It insults the AI model to force it to run faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative prompting defines strict negative boundary constraints, not emotional tone.

answer.text: It deletes all negative numbers from the manuscript's financial accounts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative prompting refers to defining what the model is prohibited from changing.

answer.text: It blocks the student from viewing the output files on GitHub.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Negative prompts guide model generation; they do not alter git repository permissions.

name.text: 08 Question: Crafting the Normalization System Prompt

questiontext.text: What are the core structural components of an effective scholarly system prompt for text normalization?

generalfeedback.text: A scholarly system prompt combines persona, task, target authority, strict negative constraints, and output formatting into an auditable protocol.

answer.text: Persona, core task, reference authority, negative constraints, and exact output formatting specifications.

feedback.text: Correct. A complete system prompt sets the editorial role, scopes the task, defines acceptable authorities, bounds forbidden actions, and fixes the output syntax.

answer.text: A Python compilation script, an operating system kernel patch, and a CSS stylesheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. System prompts are structured natural language instructions that guide LLM behavior.

answer.text: A marketing slogan, a list of student grades, and a link to the university bookstore.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompts must contain precise scholarly and computational instructions.

answer.text: A single sentence asking the model to 'make this old text look modern and clean'.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Vague instructions invite severe over-normalization and hallucination.

name.text: 09 Question: Prompt Engineering for Historical English (1752 Treaty)

questiontext.text: When prompt engineering for the 1752 Peace and Friendship Treaty, what specific rule should be enforced regarding 18th-century legal capitalization?

generalfeedback.text: Tailor prompts for 18th-century legal texts by explicitly defining rules for terminal -ck, thorn abbreviations, archaic contractions, and capitalizations.

answer.text: Preserve 18th-century substantive noun capitalization unless the explicit project policy mandates downcasing, and never let the model modernize archaic legal syntax.

feedback.text: Correct. 18th-century capitalizations reflect legal hierarchy and rhetoric; prompts must prevent the model from blindly imposing modern sentence-case rules.

answer.text: Force the model to translate all English clauses into Mi'kmaw.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The English text is being normalized according to historical English standards, not translated.

answer.text: Instruct the model to delete all references to King George II.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors never censor or alter historical political entities.

answer.text: Require the model to replace all signatures with modern digital certificates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical witness marks and signatures must be preserved diplomatically.

name.text: 10 Question: Prompt Engineering for Autograph Poetry (Emily Dickinson)

questiontext.text: Why must prompt engineering for Emily Dickinson's autograph poetry establish an absolute firewall around her dashes and punctuation?

generalfeedback.text: For Emily Dickinson's poetry, construct an aggressive poetic firewall in your prompt, strictly forbidding changes to dashes, capitalization, and lineation.

answer.text: Dickinson's dashes represent intentional rhythmic and prosodic pauses; normalizing them into standard commas or periods destroys authorial poetic form.

feedback.text: Correct. Punctuation in autograph poetry is an aesthetic component; modernizing it erases the poet's unique visual and rhythmic syntax.

answer.text: Emily Dickinson's poems were written in an unreadable binary code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dickinson wrote in 19th-century American English with distinctive autograph paleography.

answer.text: Moodle crashes whenever a poem contains an em-dash.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Moodle supports all standard Unicode dash characters.

answer.text: Publishers in the 1890s established that Dickinson's dashes were accidental ink splatters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Early publishers regularized her work, which modern scholarship rejects in favor of diplomatic fidelity.

name.text: 11 Question: Prompt Engineering for Vernacular Correspondence (Maud Lewis)

questiontext.text: What is the boundary between permissible normalization and destructive erasure in Maud Lewis's folk correspondence?

generalfeedback.text: For Maud Lewis's personal letters, instruct the AI to regularize phonetic spelling and omitted apostrophes while strictly preserving regional vernacular vocabulary.

answer.text: Regularizing phonetic spellings or missing apostrophes in contractions is permissible, but altering regional vernacular vocabulary or dialect syntax destroys her authentic voice.

feedback.text: Correct. Orthographic regularization aids searchability, but modifying dialect phrases or colloquial grammar erases working-class linguistic identity.

answer.text: All letters written by folk artists must be completely rewritten into formal academic English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Erasing vernacular grammar betrays documentary and ethnographic integrity.

answer.text: Maud Lewis's letters must be converted into French before TEI validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Maud Lewis wrote in English; translation is not normalization.

answer.text: Any letter mentioning painting must be discarded as non-historical.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lewis's discussion of her art is central to the historical value of her correspondence.

name.text: 12 Question: Prompt Engineering for Revolutionary French (1791 Decree)

questiontext.text: What historical sound change must prompts for 1791 French decrees address while protecting invariable vocabulary?

generalfeedback.text: For 18th-century French decrees, direct the model to normalize -oit imperfect verbs and accented capitals while protecting invariant homographs like droit.

answer.text: The Voltairean spelling reform shifting imperfect verb endings from -oit to -ait, while leaving nouns like droit unchanged.

feedback.text: Correct. The shift from -oit to -ait affected verb endings; nouns like droit retain the oi spelling in modern French.

answer.text: The total replacement of French with English by royal proclamation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decree was an official legislative act of the French National Assembly.

answer.text: The removal of all vowels from legal French documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. French orthography underwent gradual vowel and accent reforms, not vowel deletion.

answer.text: The conversion of all French numbers into Roman numerals.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decree used standard French numerals and cardinal words.

name.text: 13 Question: Few-Shot Prompting: Providing Examples

questiontext.text: Why does few-shot prompting dramatically improve an LLM's adherence to TEI XML normalization standards?

generalfeedback.text: Include two or three few-shot examples in your prompt to anchor the model to your exact TEI syntax and negative constraints.

answer.text: Concrete examples of input-to-output pairs demonstrate the exact XML tags, attributes, and preservation boundaries desired, grounding the model's behavior.

feedback.text: Correct. Showing the model 2-3 exact before-and-after XML demonstrations eliminates ambiguity in syntax, attribute naming, and element nesting.

answer.text: Few-shot prompting increases the hardware temperature of the computer's CPU.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Few-shot prompting provides contextual in-context training examples in the prompt text.

answer.text: Few-shot examples prevent the user from having to run git commands.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Version control operations are completely independent of prompting techniques.

answer.text: Few-shot prompting automatically compiles the XML into a PDF without software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prompting guides language model generation, not document compilation pipelines.

name.text: 14 Question: Running Normalization in VS Code Antigravity

questiontext.text: How should an editor safely execute an AI normalization pass in VS Code Antigravity?

generalfeedback.text: Execute your AI normalization pass in VS Code Antigravity by submitting your tailored prompt and consensus transcription, directing output to a dedicated candidate file.

answer.text: Run the model on clean transcription files, direct the output to a dedicated staging file (like consensus_ai.xml), and never overwrite the original ground truth directly.

feedback.text: Correct. Keeping AI outputs in an isolated file ensures the manual transcription remains pristine and allows side-by-side comparative auditing.

answer.text: Overwrite the Git repository root directory and immediately delete the commit history.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting repository history destroys provenance and academic integrity.

answer.text: Disconnect the computer from the internet and power off the monitor during generation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The editor must observe the generation process and manage the generated output.

answer.text: Run the prompt against the system kernel rather than the transcription text file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The target of normalization is the document XML transcription.

name.text: 15 Question: Formatting Output as Valid TEI <choice>

questiontext.text: What attribute should be attached to the or elements produced during an AI normalization pass to preserve methodological transparency?

generalfeedback.text: Inspect the AI output immediately to ensure it uses valid TEI <choice> element pairs, carries @resp='#gemini', and maintains well-formed XML syntax.

answer.text: resp='#gemini' (an id declared in the TEI Header), identifying the automated agent responsible for the proposed regularization.

feedback.text: Correct. Attributing machine-generated regularizations distinguishes them from human editorial decisions in the TEI markup.

answer.text: color='red'

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI semantic encoding uses @resp for responsibility, not visual display attributes.

answer.text: target='wikipedia'

feedback.text: Incorrect. Responsibility pointers reference project editors defined in the TEI Header.

answer.text: verified='true'

feedback.text: Incorrect. Machine outputs cannot self-certify their own validity.

name.text: 16 Question: Milestone Tag Preservation in AI Normalization

questiontext.text: What structural failure frequently occurs when generative LLMs process heavily marked-up TEI XML documents?

generalfeedback.text: Carefully audit the AI output to verify that every milestone tag and line number was preserved inside or adjacent to blocks.

answer.text: The model silently drops or misplaces empty milestone tags like (line breaks) and (page breaks).

feedback.text: Correct. Language models often view milestone tags as noise or lineation artifacts, omitting them unless strict prompt constraints enforce their preservation.

answer.text: The model automatically creates forty new XML namespaces.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models typically drop tags rather than inventing complex XML namespaces.

answer.text: The model converts all text into unformatted binary machine code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. LLMs output standard Unicode text strings.

answer.text:
The model replaces all

tags with HTML tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI paragraph elements are generally preserved, while empty milestones are vulnerable.

name.text: 17 Question: Conducting the Three-Way Audit (Workshop 6 Deliverable)

questiontext.text: What three files are compared during the Workshop 6 three-way normalization audit?

generalfeedback.text: The three-way audit compares your manual ground truth, deterministic regex output, and generative AI predictions to evaluate capability, precision, and fidelity.

answer.text: Manual ground truth (consensus_manual.xml), deterministic regex output (consensus_regex.xml), and AI-assisted output (consensus_ai.xml).

feedback.text: Correct. The audit triangulates human manual judgment against rule-based deterministic regex and probabilistic generative AI.

answer.text: The course syllabus, the student transcript, and the university academic calendar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The three-way audit evaluates the three computational normalization passes.

answer.text: The raw image scan, an audio recording of the lecture, and a slide deck.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The audit compares textual XML files generated under different editorial workflows.

answer.text: Three different web browsers rendering the same HTML page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The audit is a comparative philological review of encoded XML files, not a browser render check.

name.text: 18 Question: The Side-by-Side Three-Way Diff in VS Code

questiontext.text: How can editors efficiently inspect textual discrepancies between three XML versions in VS Code?

generalfeedback.text: Configure a three-column layout or run pairwise diffs in VS Code to compare your manual, regex, and AI files line by line.

answer.text: By arranging editors side-by-side across three editor columns or using pairwise diff commands ('Compare with Selected') to highlight exact token variations.

feedback.text: Correct. Visual diffing in VS Code color-codes additions, deletions, and tag shifts, making every discrepancy immediately visible.

answer.text: By printing all three files on physical paper and holding them up to a window light.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern editors use digital visual diffing tools for precision and speed.

answer.text: By deleting two of the files and guessing what differences existed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting comparative files eliminates the evidence needed for the audit.

answer.text: By reading the files backwards in terminal raw hexadecimal mode.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Side-by-side diff viewers render structured comparisons clearly.

name.text: 19 Question: Discrepancy Category A: Regex Missed, AI Caught

questiontext.text: What typically characterizes a Category A discrepancy where regex missed a form but AI correctly identified it?

generalfeedback.text: Category A discrepancies demonstrate the power of AI: models generalize across inflected endings and unpredictable spelling variations that fixed regex rules missed.

answer.text: Inflected morphological variations or unpredictable phonetic spellings that fell outside the rigid boundary of a deterministic search pattern.

feedback.text: Correct. AI models generalize across inflected endings and phonetic drift that fixed regex patterns failed to anticipate.

answer.text: The regex engine crashed due to an out-of-memory error on a single word.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regex handles single words instantly; the issue is pattern coverage, not engine memory.

answer.text: The AI model secretly accessed the original manuscript in the physical archive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model only processes the digital text provided in the prompt.

answer.text: The regex pattern was written in ancient Cuneiform script.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regex uses standard ASCII and Unicode characters.

name.text: 20 Question: Discrepancy Category B: Regex Safe, AI Hypercorrected

questiontext.text: Why does a Category B discrepancy (regex safe, AI hypercorrected) highlight the enduring strength of deterministic rules?

generalfeedback.text: Category B discrepancies demonstrate the strength of deterministic rules: regex strictly respects boundaries without hallucinating or modernizing.

answer.text: Regex strictly respects defined pattern boundaries without inventing changes, whereas the AI hallucinated or modernized words in violation of policy.

feedback.text: Correct. Deterministic regex does exactly what it is told -- no more, no less -- protecting the text against creative over-normalization.

answer.text: Regex uses artificial general intelligence to evaluate historical grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Regex is purely rule-based and deterministic, with no intelligence or semantic awareness.

answer.text: AI models are incapable of spelling any English words correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models spell modern words with high proficiency; their weakness is unwanted modernization.

answer.text: Category B discrepancies prove that computers should never be used for digital editing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Category B demonstrates the necessity of combining rule-based safety with AI discovery.

name.text: 21 Question: Discrepancy Category C: Mutual Failure and Complex Paleography

questiontext.text: What causes a Category C discrepancy where both regex and AI fail to produce the correct normalization?

generalfeedback.text: Category C discrepancies expose points of complex physical damage or poetic nuance where both regex and AI fail, requiring authoritative human judgment.

answer.text: Complex paleographical phenomena like heavily abbreviated multi-word phrases, obscure legal idioms, or ambiguous physical manuscript damage.

feedback.text: Correct. Severe manuscript degradation or rare historical idioms exceed the capacity of simple patterns and general LLM priors, demanding human expertise.

answer.text: A power outage at the local electrical substation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computational failures stem from linguistic and paleographic complexity, not power cuts.

answer.text: The TEI Consortium changing all XML specifications during the night.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas are stable international standards.

answer.text: The student accidentally opening a PDF file in an image viewer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is paleographical ambiguity within the transcribed text.

name.text: 22 Question: Calculating the Hypercorrection Rate

questiontext.text: How is the Hypercorrection Rate calculated when auditing an AI normalization pass?

generalfeedback.text: Calculate the Hypercorrection Rate (H / Total Edits) to quantify the exact frequency with which an AI model exceeded your editorial policy.

answer.text: Divide the number of hypercorrected or over-normalized tokens (H) by the total number of normalization proposals made by the model.

feedback.text: Correct. The Hypercorrection Rate (H / Total Edits) measures the proportion of model interventions that inappropriately modernized or corrupted the text.

answer.text: Multiply the number of words by the file size in megabytes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hypercorrection rate is a precision metric based on editorial error counts.

answer.text: Divide the student's grade by the number of hours spent in the computer lab.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The formula measures model error, not student time.

answer.text: Subtract the number of lines from the number of paragraphs in the TEI body.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The metric evaluates linguistic accuracy against editorial policy.

name.text: 23 Question: Evaluating Precision and Recall for the AI Pass

questiontext.text: In the context of historical text normalization, how do deterministic regex and generative AI typically compare on Precision and Recall?

generalfeedback.text: Comparing Precision and Recall reveals the fundamental trade-off: deterministic regex maximizes precision, while generative AI maximizes recall at the risk of false positives.

answer.text: Regex typically exhibits high Precision and lower Recall, while AI achieves higher Recall at the expense of lower Precision (higher false positives).

feedback.text: Correct. Regex rarely makes unauthorized edits when patterns are strict, but misses variations; AI catches almost all variants but produces unwanted hypercorrections.

answer.text: Regex and AI always produce mathematically identical Precision and Recall scores of 1.0.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Every method exhibits distinct trade-offs between coverage and error rate.

answer.text: Regex has 0% Precision because it cannot understand human feelings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Precision measures whether the executed edits were valid, which regex achieves through strict matching.

answer.text: AI has 0% Recall because it refuses to read 18th-century documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI has broad recall because it recognizes semantic variations across historical periods.

name.text: 24 Question: Synthesizing the Final Normalized Text

questiontext.text: How should an editor construct the final normalized edition (consensus_normalized.xml) from the three experimental passes?

generalfeedback.text: The final normalized file synthesizes the best of all three passes, adopting valid AI discoveries while rejecting all hypercorrections and hallucinations.

answer.text: Start with the verified manual baseline, adopt valid candidates caught by regex and AI, and reject all AI hypercorrections and hallucinated expansions.

feedback.text: Correct. The final text synthesizes the strengths of all methods: human philological judgment adjudicates candidates surfaced by rules and AI.

answer.text: Accept all AI proposals blindly without reading the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Blind acceptance imports severe hypercorrections and erases historical evidence.

answer.text: Delete all tags and keep only modern English prose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The goal is a digital edition with parallel diplomatic and normalized readings.

answer.text: Let the computer randomly select between regex and AI using a coin flip.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly editing requires reasoned, accountable decision-making.

name.text: 25 Question: Documenting AI Attribution in the TEI Header

questiontext.text: Why is documenting AI tool usage, model version, and system prompt in the an academic integrity requirement?

generalfeedback.text: Transparently attribute AI assistance in your TEI Header using <respStmt> and <change> tags, so that every @resp='#gemini' resolves to an id declared there.

answer.text: It provides a transparent computational provenance trail, allowing future scholars to understand which interventions were machine-suggested.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital humanities demands reproducible and accountable scholarship; automated interventions must be attributed and documented.

answer.text: The TEI Header is a commercial advertisement board for AI software vendors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI Header records scholarly and bibliographic metadata, not advertisements.

answer.text: Documenting AI tools automatically exempts the student from taking final exams.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Documenting methods is a standard requirement for academic rigor.

answer.text: It allows AI companies to claim legal copyright over the student's historical edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Provenance documentation records scholarly methodology; copyright rests with authorial/editorial rights.

name.text: 26 Question: Writing the Comparative Reflection Report

questiontext.text: What should form the analytical core of the Workshop 6 Comparative Reflection Report?

generalfeedback.text: Structure your 300-500 word reflection report around your policy overview, quantitative metrics table, discrepancy analysis, and lessons learned.

answer.text: A discussion of specific discrepancy categories (A, B, C) supported by quantitative metrics and philological analysis of why each method succeeded or failed.

feedback.text: Correct. The reflection must bridge quantitative metrics with deep qualitative analysis of linguistic and computational behavior.

answer.text: A summary of the weather during the week the workshop was assigned.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The report analyzes normalization methodology and textual discrepancies.

answer.text: A fictional story about an 18th-century scribe traveling through time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The assignment requires scholarly reflection on digital editing.

answer.text: A list of complaints about how difficult it is to install software.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The report focuses on editorial decisions and comparative results.

name.text: 27 Question: Ethical Dimensions of AI in Cultural Heritage

questiontext.text: What ethical danger arises when large language models are used uncritically to process minority dialects, Indigenous documents, or working-class letters?

generalfeedback.text: Digital humanists must ethically guard against AI linguistic homogenization, ensuring that automated tools preserve rather than erase non-standard historical voices.

answer.text: Linguistic homogenization, where the AI erases authentic cultural, regional, and socioeconomic voices to conform to standardized prestige dialects.

feedback.text: Correct. Generative models trained on dominant prestige dialects can homogenize unique historical voices if applied without strict ethical and editorial safeguards.

answer.text: The AI model will physically steal the paper manuscripts from museum display cases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The ethical risk is linguistic and representational, not physical theft.

answer.text: Minority languages cannot be processed by computers due to Unicode restrictions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern Unicode supports virtually all global scripts and linguistic characters.

answer.text: The AI will automatically convert all historical letters into legal copyright lawsuits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Linguistic flattening of non-standard voices is the primary cultural heritage danger.

name.text: 28 Question: Validating the Final Normalized Edition

questiontext.text: What two validation checks must the final synthesized XML file pass before submission?

generalfeedback.text: Conduct an exhaustive validation sweep before submission, ensuring your final normalized XML passes schema checks and preserves all structural tags.

answer.text: XML well-formedness (properly closed and nested tags) and TEI schema validity (compliance with project element definitions and attributes).

feedback.text: Correct. A scholarly edition must be technically well-formed and valid against the TEI schema to ensure interoperability and digital preservation.

answer.text: An internet speed test and a hard drive defragmentation check.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Validation checks verify XML structure and schema conformance.

answer.text: A copyright registration with the federal trademark office.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Technical validation is performed locally against the TEI RNG schema.

answer.text: A virus scan of the student's personal email account.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML validation evaluates the document markup itself.

name.text: 29 Question: Preparing for Week 7: Collation

questiontext.text: Why is a rigorously normalized text essential for automated collation in Week 7?

generalfeedback.text: Your normalized text provides the clean baseline needed for Week 7, where you will use CollateX to align and collate multiple historical witnesses.

answer.text: Collation algorithms (like CollateX) align texts word by word; superficial spelling variations obscure substantive textual variants unless normalized beforehand.

feedback.text: Correct. Normalization levels non-significant orthographic noise so collation algorithms can pinpoint genuine textual additions, omissions, and revisions.

answer.text: CollateX only accepts files written in modern French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CollateX works across languages once textual tokens are aligned.

answer.text: Collation software deletes all punctuation marks permanently from the repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Collation analyzes textual variance; normalization provides the necessary aligned baseline.

answer.text: Without normalization, computers refuse to boot into the operating system.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The issue is algorithmic alignment of text witnesses.

name.text: 30 Question: Review and Workshop 6 Master Checklist

questiontext.text: Which of the following packages represents the complete deliverable set for Workshop 6?

generalfeedback.text: Completing the Master Checklist guarantees that your workshop submission contains all four XML passes, a documented TEI Header, and a rigorous reflection report.

answer.text: Four valid TEI XML files (manual, regex, AI, final normalized), an updated TEI Header with AI attribution, and a Comparative Reflection Report.

feedback.text: Correct. The complete workshop package captures the full experimental trajectory and critical reflection.

answer.text: A PowerPoint presentation with twenty animated transitions and no XML files.
